## 1. Load the processed data

```{r load}
# Open the project's .Rproj file before running chunks.
# Install psych once in the Console if needed: install.packages("psych")

h1Data <- read.csv("DATA/processed_data/CLAProject_h1.csv")
h2Data <- read.csv ("DATA/processed_data/CLAProject_h2.csv")

###JK: Keep education categorical when summarizing this H1 dataset. ###
# cot_educ already contains labels such as Bachelor and Master, so as.numeric() changes all education responses to NA and hist(h1Data$educ) stops the document.
# Use table(h1Data$cot_educ) for category counts and by(h1Data$geneqavg, h1Data$cot_educ, summary) for gender-equality summaries within each education group.
# Remove the educ histograms and numerical calculations that depend on this conversion. Your summaries of geneqavg, attractimp, and commitmentavg are appropriate.
###  End of comment ###

h1Data$educ <- as.numeric((h1Data$cot_educ))


```

## 2. Look at the distribution first

```{r histogram}
# A histogram groups numerical values into intervals (bins).
# Bar height shows how many observations fall in each interval.
# Start by looking at the distribution before calculating summary statistics.
hist(h1Data$geneqavg)
  # Add readable labels to the same histogram.
    hist(h1Data$geneqavg,
         main="Distribution of gender equality attitudes",
         xlab = "Gender equality attitudes (1-7)")
    
hist(h1Data$educ)
  # Add readable labels to the same histogram.
    hist(h1Data$educ,
         main="Distribution of educational attainment",
         xlab = "Educational attainment (1-7), 1=None; 2=Primary; 3=Secondary; 4=High school/technical college; 5=Bachelor; 6=Master; 7=PhD/MD/JD or equivalent",
         cex.lab=0.4
         )

    #Histogram text size editing 
         # cex.main=0.8, # Title size
         # cex.lab=0.8, # X & Y axis label
         # cex.axis=0.7, # Axis tick numbers size
         # cex.sub = 0.7 # Subtitle size 
  
hist(h2Data$attractimp)
  # Add readable labels to the same histogram.
  hist(h2Data$attractimp,
       main="Distribution of importance of looking attractive",
       xlab = "Importance of looking attractive (1-9)")

hist(h2Data$commitmentavg)
    # Add readable labels to the same histogram.
  hist(h2Data$commitmentavg,
       main="Distribution of relationship commitment",
       xlab = "Relationship Commitment (1-5)")


```

## 3. One statistic at a time

```{r individual_statistics}
# Mean: add the scores and divide by the number of observed responses.
mean(h1Data$geneqavg, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h1Data$educ, na.rm=TRUE)


mean(h2Data$attractimp, na.rm=TRUE)
mean(h2Data$commitmentavg, na.rm=TRUE)

# Median: the middle score after sorting the responses.
median(h1Data$geneqavg, na.rm=TRUE)
median(h1Data$educ, na.rm=TRUE)

median(h2Data$attractimp, na.rm=TRUE)
median(h2Data$commitmentavg, na.rm=TRUE)

# Table: count how many people are in each category.
table(h1Data$geneqavg, useNA = "ifany")
table(h1Data$educ, useNA = "ifany")


table(h2Data$attractimp, useNA = "ifany")
table(h2Data$commitmentavg, useNA = "ifany")


# Range: return the minimum and maximum, rather than their difference.
range(h1Data$geneqavg, na.rm=TRUE)

range(h2Data$attractimp, na.rm=TRUE)
range(h2Data$commitmentavg, na.rm=TRUE)

# IQR: the 75th percentile minus the 25th percentile.
IQR(h1Data$geneqavg, na.rm=TRUE)
IQR(h1Data$educ, na.rm=TRUE)

IQR(h2Data$attractimp, na.rm=TRUE)
IQR(h2Data$commitmentavg, na.rm=TRUE)

```

## 4. Standardize a variable

```{r standardize}
# scale() uses z = (original score - mean) / standard deviation by default.
# Keep the original importance of attractiveness scores and store the standardized values separately.
# scale() returns a matrix; as.numeric() makes a simple numeric column.

# (h2Data$attractimp - mean(h2Data$attractimp,na.rm=TRUE))/sd(h2Data$attractimp,na.rm=TRUE)

h2Data$attractimp_z <- scale(h2Data$attractimp)
  #this is the function that does the same thing as the above, long written out code 

# Standardized scores have mean approximately 0 and standard deviation 1.
mean(h2Data$attractimp_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h2Data$attractimp_z, na.rm=TRUE)

# Standardize commitment avg var 
h2Data$commitmentavg_z <- scale(h2Data$commitmentavg)
  #Check 
mean(h2Data$commitmentavg_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h2Data$commitmentavg_z, na.rm=TRUE)

# Standardize gender equality attitudes avg var 
h1Data$geneqavg_z <- scale(h1Data$geneqavg)
  #Check
mean(h1Data$geneqavg_z, na.rm=TRUE)
sd(h1Data$geneqavg_z, na.rm=TRUE)

```

## 5. Covariance and correlation

```{r association}
# Covariance describes whether two variables tend to move together.
# Positive: higher values tend to occur together. Negative: higher values tend to accompany lower values.
# Its size depends on the units and is not restricted to -1 through 1.
cov(h1Data$educ, h1Data$geneqavg, use="complete.obs")

cov(h2Data$commitmentavg, h2Data$attractimp, use="complete.obs")

# Pearson correlation expresses a linear association on a -1 to 1 scale.
cor(h1Data$educ, h1Data$geneqavg, use="complete.obs")

cor(h2Data$commitmentavg, h2Data$attractimp, use="complete.obs")

# Select numerical variables only; do not include participant IDs or category codes.

corData1 <- h1Data[, c("educ", "geneqavg")]

corData2 <- h2Data[, c("attractimp", "commitmentavg")]

# A correlation matrix gives the correlation for each pair of columns.
# The diagonal is 1 because each variable is correlated with itself.

cor(corData1, use="complete.obs")

cor(corData2, use="complete.obs")


```

## 6. Several statistics at once

```{r combined_summaries}
# summary() reports minimum, quartiles, median, mean, maximum, and missing counts when present.
summary(corData1)

summary(corData2)


# psych::describe() reports n, mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, range width (max minus min), skewness, kurtosis, and other summaries.
# However it does not report every statistic above: compute IQR, cov(), and cor() separately.

psych::describe(corData1)

psych::describe(corData2)



```
